77.0.s.en: (1) A cry at the stopping of the mercies of G

77.0.0.en: 1- I cried unto God with my voice, even unto God with my voice; and he gave ear unto me.

77.0.1.en: 1- The psalmist felt great distress within himself and a strong need for God, so he cried out from his pain to God to rescue him. This shows his faith first of all, because he spoke with God and asked Him to rescue him; then the fervor of the prayer increased, and he cried out to Him. After this his faith also appears in his confidence that God gave ear to his prayer.

77.0.2.en: 2- Perhaps the psalmist felt his weakness and the multitude of his sins, so he cried out to God because he had drawn away from Him, and he asked for His swift help, His mercy and His forgiveness; and God listened attentively to his prayer. This shows God's love and His care for those who pray to Him.

77.1.0.en: 2- In the day of my trouble I sought the Lord; my hand was stretched out in the night and did not grow numb; my soul refused comfort. Grow numb: that is, it became as if under the effect of an anesthetic, so that it lost sensation (became numbed) and the ability to work. "And did not grow numb" means that it did not cease to work.

77.1.1.en: 1- When the psalmist was exposed to distress, he turned at once to God, that He might rescue him and support him, for he knows no one besides Him.

77.1.2.en: 2- In spite of the distress the psalmist continued to work, that is, to pray, to do every good thing, and to be faithful in his responsibilities, even in the night, that is, the time when everyone else rests; but the distress drove him to constructive work. And if the night is a symbol of sin, then he did not surrender to the wars of sin, but continued to strive, and his hands did not stop working.

77.1.3.en: 3- The writer continued in prayers that God might rescue him from the affliction, and his soul refused to be comforted by the words of loved ones and of all the people around him, because he was seeking comfort from God alone. In addition to this, he held fast to prayer until God should solve his problem; for he does not want comfort only, but also asks for the affliction to be lifted.

77.2.0.en: 3- I remembered God, and was troubled: I complained, and my spirit was overwhelmed. Selah.

77.2.1.en: My spirit was overwhelmed: I fainted.

77.2.2.en: 1- The psalmist expresses the extent of his distress by saying that when he prayed and remembered the name of God in order to glorify Him, his heart would open and he would tell God all his pains; he would suffer within himself and groan from the pain of soul and body, and then he would rely on God and lean upon Him.

77.2.3.en: 2- But when he does not pray and thinks about his circumstances between himself and himself, his spirit, or his inner self, cannot bear his pains, and he faints, that is, his body cannot bear the memory of the severity of his pains. This shows that they were very intense and beyond his endurance, were it not for the support of God that he receives through prayer.

77.2.4.en: 3- He ends these three previous verses with the word Selah, which is a musical pause for thinking and meditating on God, who supports us in the time of affliction.

77.3.0.en: 4- Thou holdest mine eyes waking: I am so troubled that I cannot speak.

77.3.1.en: Because of the great anxieties of the psalmist over his severe affliction, he holds the lids of his eyes, that is, he did not sleep, but kept thinking about his problems; his heart was disturbed and he was unable to speak with people, yet his conversation with God continued, as we mentioned in the previous verses. He affirms that his only comfort in affliction is in prayer. In this we see that when the psalmist thought about the affliction between himself and himself, he was troubled, because it had become beyond his endurance. This is a period of suffering he went through, or a war from Satan that made his distress of soul increase. What, then, will he do? We shall see in the following verses.

77.4.0.en: 5- I have considered the days of old, the years of ancient times.

77.4.1.en: The psalmist found the way out of his affliction, which is remembering the work of God with His people in days of old and the ancient years, that is, the former years, and how He preserved the first fathers, delivered His people from the bondage of the land of Egypt, brought them across the Red Sea, and sustained them forty years in the wilderness... In addition to remembering that God has loved him since before the foundation of the world and orders all things for his good, including afflictions. So his heart was reassured and accepted the affliction.

77.5.0.en: 6- I call to remembrance my song in the night: I commune with mine own heart: and my spirit made diligent search.

77.5.1.en: 1- When he remembered the works of God and His love, he began to sing praise, not only during the day but also at night when he was thinking, and his distress turned into joy. The night also symbolizes affliction, so his affliction was turned into rest and delight. He also remembered his happiness in God's former works, for which he sang praise and rejoiced in God.

77.5.2.en: 2- When affliction came upon the psalmist, he was not vexed with those around him who had wronged him, but he began to think and to review his feelings; as for his spirit, which believes in God, it was searching for God to intervene, that is, he was praying, asking for God to act quickly and rescue him. Thus his heart was occupied with God, so he was comforted and forgot the affliction; for solitude and meditation on God satisfy and lift a person's pains from him.

77.6.0.en: 7- Will the Lord cast off for ever? and will he be favourable no more? 8- Is his mercy clean gone for ever? doth his promise fail for evermore? 9- Hath God forgotten to be gracious? hath he in anger shut up his tender mercies? Selah. Shut up his tender mercies in anger: that is, because of His wrath He closed in upon His mercies and withheld them from us, as if they were confined in a cage.

77.6.1.en: 1- The psalmist asks: Does God reject me and become angry with me because of my sins? The proof is the presence of this affliction. But he believes that God is compassionate and merciful, and cannot forget His children and those who seek Him; so it is a rhetorical question, because he is confident that if God withdrew for a time in order to discipline us, He returns and floods His children with His love, for His mercy is limitless and never ends, and He cannot deprive His children and those who seek Him of it, and He cannot hide His voice from His people through His prophets and His righteous men, whatever their sin may be.

77.6.2.en: 2- He ends these verses with the word Selah, which is a musical pause for meditating on God's mercies that overflow upon His children.

77.7.0.en: 10- And I said, This is my infirmity: but I will remember the years of the right hand of the most High.

77.7.1.en: My infirmity: what makes me sick, that is, ill and in pain.

77.7.2.en: 1- The change of the right hand of the Most High, that is, God's mighty work with me, meaning that He shepherds me and cares for me, and then forsakes me in order to discipline me, causes me severe pain; for I have no rest or stability except in God's care for me and His mercy upon me.

77.7.3.en: 2- The change of the right hand of the Most High means the Incarnation of Christ for the redemption of mankind, and the right hand is a symbol of power, and Christ, in whom is the fullness of God's power, became incarnate to save us. But when the psalmist learned this by the spirit of prophecy, he became sick and in pain, because he also learned that his people the Jews would reject Christ and crucify Him, and consequently the hardness of heart of his people that exists now would continue until the Incarnation of Christ and would cause God to forsake them and cause them to enter into many afflictions such as the captivity.

77.7.4.en: If affliction comes upon you, hasten to God, and remember His past mercies and His provisions for your life, so that your heart may be at peace; indeed, accept the affliction that is for your good, and increase your prayers and your awareness of God, and so you will rise above the affliction.

77.8.0.en: 11- I will remember the works of the LORD: surely I will remember thy wonders of old.

77.8.1.en: 1- If God is great in His love and His gifts, then a person ought to remember His works of old, whether His marvelous ordering in His creation of man and the whole world, or His special care for His people, and His protection and care for them. All this produces reassurance and joy in the heart.

77.9.0.en: 12- I will meditate also of all thy work, and talk of thy doings.

77.9.1.en: The spiritual person is not content with remembering God's works, but also meditates on them, repeats them, and thanks God for them with all his feelings, that is, he communes with Him, and so delights in His fellowship.

77.10.0.en: 13- Thy way, O God, is in the sanctuary: who is so great a God as our God?

77.10.1.en: 1- The sanctuary is the mountain from which Moses received the commandments and the Law, and it is also the Tabernacle of Meeting where the commandments and the Law were placed. But above all this, the sanctuary is the heart of the person who loves God and keeps His commandments; there God rests and finds His way, and works freely in the person, sanctifying him, satisfying him, and revealing to him the mysteries of the Kingdom of Heaven.

77.10.2.en: 2- After experiencing God in the heart, the psalmist declares that there is no God like Him, not only in His creation of the world and man, or His care for His people, but even more in His dwelling within the heart of those who love Him, to satisfy them and make them glad.

77.11.0.en: 14- Thou art the God that doest wonders: thou hast declared thy strength among the people. 15- Thou hast with thine arm redeemed thy people, the sons of Jacob and Joseph. Selah.

77.11.1.en: 1- God's wonders were not only among His people, but appeared among all the peoples of the world, because they were great and astonishing works: He freed His people from the bondage of Egypt, then divided the Red Sea, and His people passed through it, while Pharaoh and all his army He drowned in the Red Sea; and this news spread throughout the whole world, so that after forty years Rahab the harlot, who was in Jericho, declared that she had heard of the great God of Israel, who dried up the Red Sea beneath the feet of His people (Josh 2:10).

77.11.2.en: 2- The arm of God that freed His people points to the Incarnation of Christ in the fullness of time, to free those who believe in Him from the bondage of sin.

77.11.3.en: 3- This verse ends with the word Selah, which is a musical pause for meditating on the greatness of God and His wonderful works.

77.12.0.en: 16- The waters saw thee, O God, the waters saw thee; they were afraid: the depths also were troubled.

77.12.1.en: 1- When God intervened to rescue His people at the Red Sea, when He divided it so that His people might cross through the midst of the waters on dry ground, the waters and the waves were afraid of Him and withdrew to the right and to the left to make room for the crossing of God's people; and likewise the waters of the River Jordan were afraid of God when He stopped the waters so that His people might cross in the days of Joshua, with the Ark of the Covenant.

77.12.2.en: 2- The waters and the depths are a symbol of people, who, when they beheld Christ the incarnate God, believed in Him, whether they were from the Jews or the Gentiles. And the crossing of God's people between the waters of the sea that were divided is a symbol of Baptism, in which the one baptized passes through, then comes out and is freed from his sins.

77.13.0.en: 17- The clouds poured out water: the skies sent out a sound: thine arrows also went abroad.

77.13.1.en: 18- The voice of thy thunder was in the whirlwind: the lightnings lightened the world: the earth trembled and shook.

77.13.2.en: 1- The psalmist adds details of what happened at the dividing of the Red Sea, and then when Pharaoh and his army entered after the children of Israel; he mentions that clouds appeared and rained water, and there were thunders, lightnings and an earthquake, so that the earth shook, to the point that the wheels of Pharaoh's chariots were taken off (Ex 14:25). These are additions that the psalmist declares to us, showing that God's arrows flew and sped forth, which are all these natural phenomena, to frighten Pharaoh and all his army; but he did not believe and did not fear God, and so in the end he deserved to perish and be drowned in the Red Sea.

77.13.3.en: 2- The voice of the clouds, the thunders, the lightnings and the earthquake is the voice of the Apostles and the priests of the New Testament who preached the name of Christ, so that hearts trembled before the power of the word of God, as Felix the governor trembled before the words of St. Paul the Apostle (1 v. 24:25).

77.14.0.en: 19- Thy way is in the sea, and thy path in the great waters, and thy footsteps are not known.

77.14.1.en: 1- The One who divided the Red Sea and the River Jordan is God, but the waters returned as they were, as if there had been no road or trace of God's work; yet all the peoples heard of these great events. All this was done with God's people under the leadership of Moses and Aaron, and God freed His people from the bondage of Egypt and brought them into the land of Canaan.

77.14.2.en: 2- So also throughout history God does great works, but they pass, and people forget them, like the Jews who did not realize that Christ is God, and who still do not know the footsteps of God, and His Incarnation and redemption which were preached by the Apostles, who led the believers, and who are symbolized by Moses and Aaron.

77.14.3.en: 3- Moses is the leader of the people, that is, the king and ruler, and Aaron is the priest, and they are a symbol of Christ the King and Priest who leads His people and His Church in the New Testament.

77.14.4.en: I wish that every week you would remember the works of God that He has done with you, and remember also His former works in your life and thank Him for them; then your faith will be established, your confidence in yourself will increase, and your heart will be filled with joy.

77.14.5.en: God's care and man's betrayal. A psalm of Asaph: "Give ear, O my people, to my law) "... v. 1) Introduction:

77.14.6.en: 1- Its writer: Asaph, the chief of the singers in the days of David; he was of the descendants of Levi, and was head over all the choirs of praise that the prophet David organized for singing before the house of the Lord.

77.14.8.en: a- In the days of David or immediately after him, before the division of the kingdom; because the events of this psalm stop at the age of David.

77.14.9.en: b- Some see that this psalm was written after the transfer of the Ark of the Covenant of God which was in Shiloh, which the Philistines took and which then returned to the land of the Jews, and David brought it back to Jerusalem; that is, God was pleased with His people and accepted to dwell in the midst of the holy city Jerusalem.

77.14.10.en: 3- This psalm is considered one of the historical psalms, along with Psalms 105, 106, 107, 135 and 136.

77.14.11.en: 4- This psalm is considered the second in length, after Psalm 119, the longest of the psalms.

77.14.12.en: 5- The aim of this psalm is to show God's care and concern for His people, from the time He brought them out of the bondage of the land of Egypt, then how He took care of them in the wilderness of Sinai, and took care of them in the land of Canaan until the great David reigned over them. In contrast, it shows the extent of the betrayal of God's people and of their servants toward Him, and their forgetting of His commandments and His worship, so that they deserved punishment.

77.14.13.en: 6- The New Testament quoted from this psalm, as in:

77.14.17.en: 7- This psalm is not found in the prayer of the Agpeya.

77.14.18.en: (5) The necessity of keeping the commandments (1-8:)
